This is something I've been wondering for a while. I've been taking courses and messing around with C++. Most of the courses I take tell me of "established practices" and things that developers absolutely hate (such as using namespaces). They also talk a lot about practicing encapsulation and thinking using abstraction. It seems that this would become more muddled as the language becomes higher level thus making code harder to understand without comments explicitly saying what's happening in a function.

While C++ has gone through several iterations (as well as other languages) I'm wondering that, if in the process of this, if developers have become better at making encapsulated code or if it's gotten worse with progressively more powerful languages and led to code that requires more explanation to understand.

Basically, as languages have become higher level, have we started to see more or less understandable code?
Are programs today easier to understand than the beginning of programming?

With each level of abstraction a program becomes less understandable at the hardware level but more understandable at the abstract level.

When languages get a new version, usually new features get added but none removed for backwards compatibility. So one might say the new versions are less understandable based on this. But the new features are usually simplifying things because developers want that, so one might agree with that otherwise.

For deeper insight

Moving from assembly and a mess of gotos and jumps to if and other statements improves source code. Spaghetti code: bad. This is why languages around the level of C are (or were) popular. Hiding what a program does through layers of abstraction and indirection worsens source code. Classes in many languages are an example (python being my pet peeve right now). They can extend what another class does but stack them up so much and you have to look at a dozen documentation pages to see the features available in in one.

In other words there is a peak of understandability where the abstraction has moved sufficiently far from the hardware but before it gets buried under layers of further abstraction.

(Not that I have ever been educated in CS.)

Took a long drive this morning and saw two things a few times that completely screwed the flow of traffic and spent time thinking how to stop it.

First thing I saw was people getting on the freeway and immediately shooting over to the fast lane and then accelerating. This caused a ton of braking and overall slowdown in the middle and left lane. Then there was their brothers in spirit who went from the far left lane all the way to the exit at the last possible moment with pretty much the same effect.

The other thing I saw a few times, usually when someone was traveling below the flow of traffic in the center lane, was two cars attempting to merge into the center lane from the left and right lane at the same time. Everyone around sees the possibility for a collision and slows down to give themselves lots of room so they don't have to join that party.

So what are the benefits of the alternating lines? First, it forces people get up to the speed of their own lane before changing to a faster lane. Second, it removes the possibility of two people from the outside lanes merging into the same gap in the center lane. Third, it forces people to pay more attention and think their route ahead and move inside as their exit approaches. Fourth it gives people passing a sense of urgency when passing someone to give it some gas and get in front of someone instead of a slow 4mph difference pass.

In my mind it would be two stages between most exits. When you get on the freeway you'd be greeted with a solid line to your left. This is the area you'd get up to speed if you didn't already on the on ramp and this is also the area people from the fast lane would start moving over for the next exit. At the mid point you'll get your striped lines to move to a faster lane and people can move over again for their exit. And finally between the exit and next entrance you'll have striped lines to your left and you can make it to the passing/fast lane if you wish.

Obviously you're gonna have plenty of people ignoring the lines altogether, I see it all the time with the HOV lane, but enough people follow the rules that I think it could make a big difference.

Thoughts? Criticisms?
